Microevolution and macroevolution are terms used to describe different levels of evolutionary change.
Microevolution refers to small-scale changes that occur within a species or population over a relatively short period of time.

These changes involve variations in the frequencies of alleles (different forms of genes) within a population, and can result from processes such as genetic drift, mutation, gene flow, and natural selection.
Examples of microevolutionary changes include the evolution of antibiotic resistance in bacteria or the development of pesticide resistance in insects.
Macroevolution, on the other hand, refers to larger-scale changes that occur over longer periods of time and can lead to the formation of new species or higher taxonomic groups.

These changes may involve the evolution of new body structures or the development of new functions, and can result from a combination of microevolutionary processes and other factors such as geographic isolation, hybridization, or major environmental changes.
Examples of macroevolutionary changes include the evolution of whales from land-dwelling mammals or the evolution of birds from theropod dinosaurs.
While microevolution and macroevolution are distinct concepts, they are not completely separate processes, and the two are linked by a continuum of evolutionary change.
